content:
A familiar Christian reading of the Gospels holds that Jesus (peace be upon him) "broke" the Sabbath, and with it the Law of Moses, so that his followers were set free from both. John 5:18 seems to say as much: "he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father".[1]

The Gospels tell a fuller story. Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath "as was his custom" (Luke 4:16), and each Sabbath dispute they record turns on what the commandment allows, with the commandment itself taken for granted.[2]

This article aims to provide context to that reading, insha'Allah, in five Sabbath controversies, read against the Torah and the Jewish law of the time. The Quran gives the frame: Jesus came "to attest the Law which was before me. And to make lawful to you part of what was (before) forbidden to you" (3:50).[3]

"He was going on the Sabbath day through the grain fields, and his disciples began, as they went, to pluck the ears of grain. The Pharisees said to him, 'Behold, why do they do that which is not lawful on the Sabbath day?'" (Mark 2:23 to 24).[4]

The charge was work on the Sabbath, and theft had nothing to do with it. The Torah allowed a hungry passer-by to pluck grain by hand: "you may pluck the ears with your hand; but you shall not move a sickle to your neighbor's standing grain" (Deuteronomy 23:25). The question was whether plucking counted as reaping.[5]

Jesus answers with David, who ate the holy bread when he was hungry, and with a principle: "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27).[4] The argument is about the purpose of the commandment, made from inside the Torah.

In Mark 3:1 to 6 a man with a withered hand stands in the synagogue, and Jesus asks: "Is it lawful on the Sabbath day to do good, or to do harm? To save a life, or to kill?"[4]

Jewish law already set the Sabbath aside to save a life. The Mishnah rules that wherever there is doubt whether a life is in danger, that doubt overrides the Sabbath.[6] A withered hand was no threat to life. The harder question, then and later, was treatment that could wait a day. Nina Collins's study of Sabbath healing in the first and second centuries argues that the Gospel healing stories preserve part of a Jewish debate on this question that ran from the second century BCE to the end of the second century CE, and that the sages allowed healing on the Sabbath throughout it. On her reading, Jesus' arguments belong to that debate.[7]

In Luke 13:10 to 17 the ruler of the synagogue objects: "There are six days in which men ought to work. Therefore come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day!"[8]

Jesus answers from common practice: "Doesn't each one of you free his ox or his donkey from the stall on the Sabbath, and lead him away to water? Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?"[8] If an animal may be loosed for water, a daughter of Abraham may be loosed from her illness.

Luke 14:1 to 6 sets the next healing in the house of a leading Pharisee, at a Sabbath meal. After healing a man with dropsy, Jesus asks the lawyers: "Which of you, if your son or an ox fell into a well, wouldn't immediately pull him out on a Sabbath day?"[8]

The scene is a meal among Pharisees, and the argument is one they could follow, from the lesser case to the greater. The Gospel shows Jesus and the Pharisees sharing the commandment and disputing its application.

In John 5 Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years and tells him: "Arise, take up your mat, and walk." The objection is to the carrying: "It is the Sabbath. It is not lawful for you to carry the mat."[1]

John turns the dispute toward Jesus' relation to God. "My Father is still working, so I am working, too," and the opponents seek to kill him "because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God" (John 5:17 to 18).[1] Steven Bryan reads the healing as a sign through which John introduces the discourse on the Father and the Son that follows.[9]

The words "he broke the Sabbath" give the charge of the opponents, in a Gospel written to make a claim about Jesus' person. They are the accusation the chapter answers.

The bottom line

The five controversies are arguments over how to keep the Sabbath: whether plucking grain is reaping, whether healing that could wait may be done, whether a bent woman may be loosed as an ox is. In each, Jesus argues from the Torah's own purpose, at the synagogue and at the Pharisee's table, and he says of the Law: "I didn't come to destroy, but to fulfill" (Matthew 5:17).[10] Sunday worship is a later development; the Catechism of the Catholic Church presents Sunday as fulfilling the spiritual truth of the Sabbath.[11]

The Quran gives Jesus exactly this role, a prophet who confirms the Torah and lightens some of its burdens (3:50). It says of the Sabbath that it "was only made (strict) for those who disagreed (as to its observance)" (16:124). Islam has no Sabbath of its own: the Muslims are told to "leave off business" for the Friday prayer, and "when the Prayer is finished, then may ye disperse through the land, and seek of the Bounty of Allah" (62:9 to 10).[3] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. John 5:1 to 18 (World English Bible).
  2. Luke 4:16 (World English Bible).
  3. Quran 3:50; 16:124; 62:9 to 10, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  4. Mark 2:23 to 3:6; Matthew 12:1 to 14; Luke 6:1 to 11 (World English Bible).
  5. Deuteronomy 23:25 (World English Bible).
  6. Mishnah Yoma 8:6.
  7. Nina L. Collins, Jesus, the Sabbath and the Jewish Debate: Healing on the Sabbath in the 1st and 2nd Centuries CE (London: Bloomsbury T&T Clark, 2014).
  8. Luke 13:10 to 17; 14:1 to 6 (World English Bible).
  9. Steven M. Bryan, "Power in the Pool: The Healing of the Man at Bethesda and Jesus' Violation of the Sabbath (Jn. 5:1-18)", Tyndale Bulletin 54.2 (2003), 7 to 22.
  10. Matthew 5:17 to 18 (World English Bible).
  11. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2174 to 2176.
